stories.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
stories.summary: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU

Published 15 November 2026

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

Exit clause

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

Contentious crisp flavourings

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

Salon owner: 'We have parents offering to pay their kids' wages'

Published 15 November 2026

National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge.

There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show.

Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest.

Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any.

Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill

Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full.

He has already unveiled some of his proposals including:

Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales

A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits.

Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270.

However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000.

This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase.

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

Milburn told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.

"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.

"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."

On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.

People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.

McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".

stories.title: Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says
stories.summary: Russell Brand's barrister has been accused of peddling rape myths while defending the comedian.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Alex Norris said the perpetuation of such myths in a court room is "unacceptable"

Published 16 November 2026

The justice secretary has called for new rules to prevent barristers from using rape myths to defend their clients in the wake of the Russell Brand trial.

As first reported by the Times , external , in a letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Alex Norris said it was "unacceptable" to "perpetuate myths" about victims in court and disciplinary action could be taken against those who do so.

In his closing speech, Brand's defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why his client's accusers had not fought back.

The BSB said it had set up an expert group this year to advise on "strengthening standards for barristers", while the Bar Council said defendants had a "right to have evidence tested in court".

Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says Published 8 hours ago

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

In an interview with the BBC earlier this month, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said some of the comments made at the trial he had seen reported were "getting very close to victim blaming".

He also backed calls for a law change that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure victims of rape cases do not feel like they are on trial .

stories.body:
Long-awaited final report will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis

‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking

A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age.

On Tuesday, Alan Milburn’s final report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction.

It will be a big test for Andy Burnham’s government. Milburn will call for controversial benefit cuts for under-25s in exchange for a legal guarantee of a job or training. Alongside changes to education and health, his plan will take a decade to implement.

Behind his argument is a principle Labour has struggled with – that restricting benefits to encourage work is a good idea.

The system clearly is not working. Milburn makes the case eloquently – pointing out that for every £1 spent on job support £25 goes on benefits. But there are also important caveats: change will count for nothing unless employers play their part; half of all Neets are not on benefits, and bad jobs and a lack of entry-level opportunities are far bigger drivers of Britain’s youth jobs crisis than the generosity of the benefits system.

Last week, the Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told me Britain’s young people were bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” , with employers freezing recruitment amid the war in the Middle East.

Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis to reach its highest level relative to the total for all ages since the early 1990s. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment.

All of this compounds a drop in entry-level jobs over the past two decades. The Saturday job died long ago, while to make matters worse, those positions at the start of the career ladder are most at risk of automation or replacement by AI.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the places in Britain with the fewest job vacancies have the highest Neet rates. Highlighting stark regional divisions, young jobseekers in Rotherham face a sixfold gap in opportunity relative to their peers in the Cotswolds.

The preferred fixes called for by employers are tax cuts, looser regulations, and holding back rises in the youth minimum wage. But while policy costs are unquestionably a factor to consider, and the state could do more to help young people get ready for work, the problems go much deeper.

When Milburn’s report comes out, corporate Britain will be out in force to show willing. Amazon, Marks & Spencer, Shell and Pret a Manger are among those who have already spotted the PR opportunity to showcase their efforts. But most are doing nowhere near enough.

Of course it costs time and money to run youth outreach programmes, work experience schemes and to help recruits who need support to get up to speed – especially in tough economic times. But the consequences from not doing so are becoming increasingly clear.

Almost half of jobseekers under 25 surveyed by the organisation Youth Employment UK think employers were unsupportive. Stories of the applications black holes and the catch-22 of companies demanding experience – even for entry-level roles – are all too commonplace.

In Britain’s youth jobs crisis, issues with the quality of work on offer and opportunities for progression also play a part. Low paid, insecure jobs are rife – most notably in places with the highest Neet rates. Over the past quarter of a century in-work poverty has increased. Among working households, the relative poverty rate is almost a fifth (18%) compared with 13% in the mid-1990s.

Figures this month show people’s job satisfaction has dropped to the lowest level recorded by the British Social Attitudes survey. Among young people it is particularly gloomy: separate figures show most believe that not everyone can go as far as their talent and hard work will take them.

after newsletter promotion

Young people are more likely to find insecure work , only to end up jobless again within weeks. More than one in 10 are on zero-hours contracts. For many that flexibility is welcome and can be launchpad to a career – a point seized on by employers’ groups. But despite the gig economy boom of the past 25 years, Britain’s Neet rate has only fallen below 10% once.

Countless studies show badly paid and insecure work is linked to poor mental wellbeing . Across all types of jobs, almost 1 million people in Britain suffer from work-related stress, depression or anxiety . But those in poor-quality employment are up to three times more likely to leave the workforce than those in the highest-quality positions.

For the growing number of Neets grappling with mental health problems the prospect of entering a labour market like this is daunting.

Milburn’s view is that, despite these challenges, emphasising participation is unequivocally the right thing to do. With extra support the barriers to work could be overcome.

The argument is getting a job is better than life sitting in a bedroom doomscrolling . Work can give structure, routine, social connects, status and – here’s hoping – some financial security. On the flipside, unemployment is a killer for wellbeing and financially ruinous.

For those who reach the age of 24 without ever having had a job, even if they successfully re-enter the labour market, they stand to lose up to £300,000 in lifetime earnings.

Like most people, the young want to work. Across society as few as 4% of working-age adults say they would ideally prefer not to – dropping to just 2% of under-25s.

But fixing the social contract will require more than benefit cuts and a 10-year overhaul of the state. There is a big job, too, for employers.

stories.summary: As a landmark report about youth unemployment is about to be published, the BBC speaks to school avoiders and those trying to fix the issue.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

'It felt like I was dying’: Why some teenagers don’t go to school

Published 16 November 2026

Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.

She describes how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.

"It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she recalls.

"If I was able to get in the car, we'd drive to school," she continues. "I'd probably normally either faint or throw up while we were sat in the car park."

Eva's one of the thousands of school pupils in England who misses more than half the academic year. Experts say that children who miss school are more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training. A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday.

Eva is autistic and stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education.

Every morning, one of Eva's parents would call her teachers to tell them she wouldn't be going in that day, and she says she would stay at home watching YouTube videos and episodes of Horrible Histories "just to try and keep up".

Eva, 13, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary school

This year, she has started at an alternative provision school which has smaller class sizes, therapy animals and more freedom to take breaks. But she still worries about her future and whether her record of school avoidance might turn off future employers.

Eva recognises that many older people will assume "tough love" is the answer, and that they might even call pupils like her lazy - but she believes the situation is more complex.

"We're not lazy, we want to go, we want to do something, we want to live our lives, but we can't," she says.

Eva now attends an alternative provision school with smaller class sizes

Total school absence numbers have fallen since their peak during the pandemic but they're yet to return to pre-Covid levels.

In the autumn and spring terms of the 2025/26 academic year, the overall absence rate was 6.6%, down from 7.38% in 2021/2022 but much higher than pre-pandemic levels, which were below 5%.

The latest figures published in October show that 168,000 pupils (2.32%) were classed as severely absent - missing more than half of their classes - in the 2025/2026 autumn and spring terms. Back in spring 2019, this figure was under 60,000.

Experts are concerned that this absence will translate into worse outcomes for thousands of young people.

New analysis from the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) shows that 133,000 of today's persistently absent GCSE pupils (those missing more than 10% of school) are on course to spend a year or more being Neet. Similar research from the National Centre for Social Research linked persistent absence to much higher rates of not being in work, education or training between the ages of 16 and 24.

"Ministers must recognise that getting children back into school is the first step to getting young people into work," says Dan Lilley, head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.

"That means restoring the expectation that children are in school every day."

Research suggests many parents may be comfortable with regular school absences. CSJ polling found that 44% of parents think it reasonable for a child to miss one in every 10 school days – the threshold for persistent absence.

In response to the CSJ research, the Department for Education said it was "helping tackle the barriers that stop children attending school, through free breakfast clubs in every primary school, better mental health support and earlier help for pupils with special educational needs".

Autism and ADHD can contribute to children avoiding school, says Sheila Griffiths, who co-founded the charity Hope4More in Crewe after her own son struggled to attend school.

"The classroom environment doesn't suit [those children], so we support them here," she explains.

Hope4More runs art classes that combine creativity and business skills, and it also supports parents to ask for the help they need from schools or their local authority to get their child back into education.

"We've got families here who have already had to give up work. They're struggling. It's so stressful the situations they end up in."

Sheila also runs a programme at Cheshire College South & West to help young people with the transition into further education.

She says: "With our older ones, so perhaps the ones that should be in year 10 or 11, we work with them at college and then they get used to being in that environment which is different to school, but it's also still quite busy."

Paul Browne, who is one of the assistant principals there, says: "Especially since Covid, there's a lot of learners who are not engaging in education. The thought of coming into a mainstream college is quite a big step for them.

Paul Browne is an assistant principal at Cheshire College South & West

"We're seeing [most of] our students now are more like they were before Covid, where doing exams and coming to college is the norm. But there's still that small cohort [who struggle] and it's about getting them ready and helping them back into education."

Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago in year 10.

"We didn't do our Sats because that's when the first lockdown hit," she recalls.

"It was so isolating and so strange, but I loved it. I was able to sit in my own room and do schoolwork.

"Going back into school, it was difficult. I started struggling with panic attacks a lot, to the point where I was being pulled out of classes."

Mali was diagnosed with autism when she was 15. After she stopped attending school, her mental health deteriorated to the point where she didn't leave her bedroom.

"It was like the second I got past my doorframe, my whole body would stop. My legs would go numb, my head would tense. It felt like I was dying. I can't explain it any other way."

She still doesn't leave the house.

"I do get quite emotional about it. I feel like I've tried so hard and I went to school for so long and I went through so much and I have nothing to show for it. I don't have my GCSEs, I didn't even do my Sats."

stories.body:
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.

Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.

“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”

German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.

“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine , and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron , warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.

“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta , in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.

“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.

“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.

“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo . It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.

More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

stories.title: Workers should get paid time off to train for crises, say peers
stories.summary: A House of Lords committee says more preparation is needed for war, power cuts, and cyber-attacks.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 November 2026

Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended.

In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income.

It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters.

It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies.

In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step".

But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks.

It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters.

The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic.

'Proportionate' leave

It noted that the previous government floated the idea of a "civilian reservist cadre" to help out in times of crisis in its 2021 defence review, but this was dropped when the report was updated two years later.

Although some employers offer time off to staff who volunteer, there is currently no legal entitlement to paid leave for those in roles such as coastguard rescue, firefighting, or the St John Ambulance.

Army reservists can claim up to £400 a day , external from the government to cover lost pay if they are mobilised, but employers do not have to allow time off for training - although some choose to do so.

In their report, the peers said a new right to paid time off could cover "approved" training and volunteering, without specifying exact roles.

They did not recommend an exact leave entitlement, instead suggesting that Labour ministers should work with employers to design "proportionate arrangements" for workers.

New preparedness app

Elsewhere in their report, peers recommended the government should send booklets to every household with information about what to do in a crisis, modelled on those sent to homes in Sweden and Denmark.

In its evidence to the inquiry, the government said it planned to provide information through its website - but peers rejected this approach, adding it risked "excluding some groups" and would not work during prolonged periods of disruption.

The peers also recommended the development of a multilingual "public preparedness app" to access official guidance on preparing for emergencies.

It should also allow users to automatically share their location with emergency authorities, similar to the 112 Suomi app in Finland, they added.

The Cabinet Office said it would "carefully review" the report, whilst insisting the government was already taking action to improve crisis resilience.

It pointed to work already under way to update departments' secret defence plans, known as the "war book", and a major exercise scheduled for next year to test the the UK's resilience for war.

The government also recently announced new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables, including powers for officials to inspect cable landing stations owned and operated by telecom companies.

stories.title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
stories.summary: Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone , a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem , plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company . What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks. How much home usage data this is based on, and if it can be used to infer when certain household activities are happening, are both open questions. And presumably, to maintain the preset routes, inferred data about your home will still be held by Ring even after any stored video footage is deleted. The risk to your privacy is only compounded once you consider Ring’s renewed partnership with police through the massive surveillance and taser vendor, Axon. Through this partnership, police have the ability to request camera footage from Ring users with just a few clicks on Axon’s platforms. This includes its Fusus platform , an interactive surveillance feed and map police use to manage all the surveillance devices they have access to, like automated license plate readers . It’s unclear exactly what devices police can request footage from, but if this request feature is extended to Ring’s drones, police could easily send requests for footage from inside your house. Sharing is voluntary, but once footage is submitted, it cannot be retracted. Worse still, if your footage is not sitting on Amazon’s servers fully encrypted—and there’s reason to believe their privacy options are not the strongest —police could serve a warrant straight to the company, instead of to you, to get footage from…

stories.summary: In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.
